            Bio
            Hello world! I am a Collegiate
            Assistant Professor at the University of Chicago, where
            I teach Global Society in the College
            Core. Trained as a quantitative social scientist, I do
            interdisciplinary research on demography and population
            health.
            Before joining the University of Chicago, I was a
            postdoctoral scholar at the Center for
            Economic History at Northwestern University. I have a
            PhD in Sustainable
            Development from Columbia University.
            Off campus, you’re most likely to find me wilderness canoeing, enjoying
            the Chicago lake
            shore, or reading sci-fi and fantasy (current
            recommendation).

articles.title: Research
articles.contents:
I study population health in data-scarce settings. One side of my work develops childhood sex ratios as a proxy for early-life mortality: because boys die at higher rates in infancy, the sex composition of surviving children carries a mortality signal that a census can recover even when we lack vital statistics. I apply this novel indicator to the historical US, where we lack vital statistics but have excellent census data.
Another strand of my work focuses on maternal-infant health in contemporary sub-Saharan Africa, based on Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) data.
Publications
Infant Mortality among US Whites in the 19th Century:
New Evidence from Childhood Sex Ratios
with James R. Irwin · Demographic Research. 2025.

Uses childhood sex ratios, which skew female when infant mortality is high, to
estimate 19th-century US infant mortality. Estimates for US whites are roughly
70–80 deaths per 1,000 in the mid-1800s.


Demographic Research 52: 303–350.

Child Anemia and the 2008 Food Price Crisis in Senegal ·
Demographic Research. 2024.

Examines how the 2008 food price crisis affected child hemoglobin in Senegal,
using a quasi-experimental comparison of in-utero and breastfeeding children.
Urban areas, especially Dakar, saw large negative effects, while rural areas
showed none.


Demographic Research 51: 637–668.

Working Papers
The Hidden Costs of Mass Deportations:
Early-Life Mortality and the 1930s Mexican Repatriation
with Sergio Eduardo López Araiza Bejar (October 2026)

The repatriation campaigns of the 1930s removed a large share of the Mexican-origin
population of the United States, including many US-born children. We use childhood
sex ratios to estimate the effect on early-life mortality among Mexican immigrants in Texas.
We find that the campaign caused a major shift towards females among the affected population,
implying a large increase in early life mortality.


Draft

Works in Progress
Black Health in Slavery and Freedom: New Evidence from Childhood Sex Ratios.
With James R. Irwin. Estimates infant mortality among US Black and white populations,
1850–1880, using childhood sex ratios and European vital statistics.
Comparing the JMP Drinking Water Ladder and the HWISE Scale in the 2022–23
Mozambique DHS. With Sera Young and Indira Bose. Compares an infrastructure-based
and an experience-based measure of household water access in a single survey.
Solving the Antebellum Puzzle: New Evidence from Childhood Sex Ratios.
Sex Ratio at Birth and the HIV Epidemic in South Africa. With Jenny Trinitapoli.

articles.title: Teaching
articles.contents:
I teach the Global Society sequence in the College Core at the University of Chicago. My courses move students from consuming research to producing it: the course ends in an independent research project built on real data.
Classes Designed

The Demographic History of the US post 1860 
(ECON 323-2) at Northwestern University (Winter 2025)

Listed in the catalogue as Economic History of the United States since 1865; I designed and taught it as a course in demographic history.


This course examines the demographic history of the US from after the Civil War to the mid 20th century. Students learn core demographic concepts and measures, like fertility and mortality rates. They explore the demographic patterns and changes in the United States. They examine leading theories for fertility and mortality decline, as well as exploring the role of immigration in US history. Students learn to analyze publicly available census microdata from IPUMS, culminating in an independent research project.

Classes Taught

Global Society I, II and III 
(SOSC 16100 / 16200 / 16300) at the University of Chicago (2025–present)

A three-quarter Core social sciences sequence, which I teach in two sections each year. The first two quarters work through foundational texts on development, inequality and population, with quantitative labs in the winter quarter that introduce students to working with data directly. The third quarter is a research practicum: each student develops an independent project from question formulation through to a 6,000-word paper.


Global Society III: Research Practicum 
(SOSC 16300) at the University of Chicago (2023–2024)

This course introduces students to the process of doing academic research, and moving from being consumers to producers of knowledge. My section focused on demographic research in a global context, including fertility, mortality and immigration. Students developed independent research projects with my guidance, culminating in a mini research paper.


Methods in Global Health 
(ANT 390) at Northwestern University (2025)

A seminar on quantitative and qualitative methods in global health research, co-taught with Sera Young. I led the statistical computing component, teaching students to work with survey data in R and to evaluate measurement choices in global health indicators.
